utterance: Two more things I need to check. At any point since it started, did the pain suddenly get much worse or spread across your whole tummy? And have you had a sore throat, a cough or a feverish illness in the last week or two?

utterance: Samuel, here's what I think is going on. Your pain started around your belly button and moved down to the right lower side, you've lost your appetite and been sick, you've got a temperature of 37.9 and a fast pulse, and when I press on that right lower area — and when you cough or I percuss it — it's very sore. Your urine and the rest of your tummy are reassuring, and your testicles are normal. That pattern is very typical of an inflamed appendix — appendicitis. I can't be 100% certain without scans and blood tests, but I'm not willing to sit and watch this, because if an appendix bursts it can cause a serious infection spreading through the tummy. So I've given you an injection of morphine for the pain, and I want you to go to the emergency department now to be seen by the surgeons — they'll do blood tests and a scan and decide whether you need an operation, usually a keyhole one. Please don't eat or drink anything from now on in case you need an anaesthetic, don't take any laxatives or painkillers at home, and don't drive yourself. Is there someone who can drive you to the hospital right now?
reply: Yeah, my brother's coming. He'll drive me.

awards.label: Phone the emergency department with a handover
Refer to the emergency department today for surgical assessment

utterance:
Right, here's the plan and what you need to know.

1. I've rung the emergency department and given them a handover about you, so they're expecting you. Go straight there now with your brother — please don't drive yourself. The morphine I've given you can make you drowsy, so no driving and no operating machinery or working at heights for the next 24 hours.

2. Nothing to eat or drink from now on — not even water — until the hospital team say it's okay. That's in case you need an anaesthetic.

3. Don't take laxatives or enemas, and don't just take painkillers at home and wait this out.

4. I've sent off a full blood count and a CRP (inflammation marker); those results will go to the hospital and I'll get a copy too. Your urine dipstick showed only trace blood and white cells and no infection, which is reassuring against a urine or kidney problem.

5. At hospital they'll examine you, do bloods and a scan — ultrasound or a CT — and if it is your appendix you'll get antibiotics and usually a keyhole operation to remove it. Most people go home in a day or two and are back to normal in a couple of weeks, though you'll need some time off work and off tools — I can write you a certificate.

6. Call 000 straight away, on the way there or at any point, if the pain suddenly becomes much worse or spreads across your whole tummy, if you keep vomiting, if you get a high temperature or shaking chills, if you feel faint, cold and clammy or confused, or if your tummy becomes hard and swollen. Those are signs the appendix may have burst.

7. And if the hospital sends you home saying it isn't appendicitis, but the pain gets worse or isn't clearly settling over the next day or two, come back and see me or return to the emergency department — early appendicitis sometimes only declares itself later, and I'd rather you were checked again.

This is a very treatable problem and you're doing the right thing by getting it seen today. The sooner it's dealt with, the less chance of complications.
reply: I'll go with my brother. He'll drive me.

awards.label: Not a can't-miss diagnosis here: Sepsis
